snip.t: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a chronic, progressive, degenerative joint disease characterised by loss of articular cartilage, sub‑chondral bone remodelling, osteophyte formation and synovial inflammation, leading to pain, stiffness and functional limitation.
Osteoarthritis is by far the most common type of arthritis.
Rheumatology — rheumatoid arthritis; SLE; gout and other crystal arthropathies; osteoarthritis; systemic sclerosis; vasculitis; inflammatory myopathies; septic arthritis; spondyloarthritis.

snip.t: | Musculoskeletal (Osteoarthritis) | Pain on joint motion, weight-bearing, or morning stiffness | Pain tied to mechanical joint load, not walking distance; pulses intact |
Musculoskeletal: Joint line tenderness, limited ROM — Obesity stresses weight‑bearing joints, may reveal early osteoarthritis.
Musculoskeletal: Osteoarthritis, gout — Reduced mobility, chronic pain
| Osteoarthritis | Age >50, mechanical pain, worsens with use, no morning stiffness | Asymmetric, non‑inflammatory, no systemic features, normal inflammatory markers |

qs.q: What is the classic duration that distinguishes morning stiffness in rheumatoid arthritis from osteoarthritis?
o: More than one hour in rheumatoid arthritis versus less than half an hour in osteoarthritis
Less than fifteen minutes in rheumatoid arthritis versus several hours in osteoarthritis
Exactly thirty minutes in both rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis conditions
Only upon heavy exertion for both rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis conditions
qs.e: Morning stiffness is prolonged in rheumatoid arthritis lasting more than one hour, whereas in osteoarthritis it lasts less than half an hour. Shorter durations are not characteristic of active rheumatoid inflammation.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Osteoarthritis is a degenerative joint disease causing mechanical pain that improves with rest and joint crepitus. It results from cartilage loss and subchondral bone changes, most often in weight‑bearing joints.

sections.p: A chronic, progressive loss of articular cartilage with secondary bone remodeling causing pain, stiffness and functional limitation.
b: Diagnosis is clinical; radiographs show joint space narrowing, osteophytes, subchondral sclerosis, and cysts.

t.a: Plain radiograph (X‑ray) of the affected joint
t.b: Does the joint show space loss, osteophytes, sclerosis? Positive findings confirm structural OA; a normal X‑ray does not exclude early disease.
Is the effusion inflammatory or infected? Clear, non‑inflammatory fluid supports primary OA; purulent fluid mandates infection work‑up.

sections.p: Severity is graded by symptoms and radiographic changes (Kellgren‑Lawrence 0‑4).
b: Stage 0–1: doubtful narrowing, minimal symptoms.
Stage 2: definite osteophytes, mild‑moderate pain.
Stage 3: multiple osteophytes, moderate joint space loss, functional limitation.
Stage 4: severe narrowing, bone‑on‑bone, marked disability.

sections.p: Most cases are primary (age‑related) but secondary causes accelerate cartilage loss.
b: Primary aging and biomechanical wear (most common).
Obesity – increased load on knees, hips, spine.
Joint malalignment (varus/valgus) or previous trauma.
Metabolic disorders (hemochromatosis, gout).
Infection‑related secondary OA (post‑septic arthritis, TB joint).
Chronic inflammatory diseases (rheumatoid arthritis, seronegative spondyloarthropathy).

sections.p: Patients report joint pain that worsens with activity and improves with rest, morning stiffness <30 min, crepitus, and reduced range of motion.
b: Knee: pain on climbing stairs, palpable grinding with patellar compression.
Hip: groin pain, limp, limited internal rotation.
Hand: Heberden’s (distal) and Bouchard’s (proximal) nodes.

sections.p: Imaging and fluid analysis confirm structural disease and exclude mimics.

t.b: Shows joint space narrowing and osteophytes; confirms OA severity.
Detects early cartilage loss, meniscal tears, or subchondral edema; useful when surgery is considered.
Rules out septic arthritis or crystal arthropathy; clear fluid supports OA.

sections.p: Identify features that suggest alternative serious pathology or severe disease.
b: Rapidly progressive pain, swelling, fever – consider septic arthritis or inflammatory arthritis.
Night pain unrelieved by rest – possible malignancy or infection.
Severe deformity or loss of function – may need surgical referral.

sections.p: Treat underlying risk factors, relieve pain, preserve function, and plan for eventual joint replacement if needed.
b: Weight reduction (5–10 % body weight) to lower joint load.
Physical therapy: quadriceps strengthening, range‑of‑motion exercises.
Topical NSAIDs for mild pain; oral NSAIDs if needed, avoiding in renal disease or peptic ulcer.
Acetaminophen for analgesia when NSAIDs contraindicated.
Intra‑articular corticosteroid injection for acute flare; limit to 3‑4 per year.
Viscosupplementation (hyaluronic acid) in selected knee OA when other measures fail.
Joint replacement when pain persists despite maximal conservative therapy.

sections.p: Regular review of symptoms, function, and risk‑factor control.
b: Re‑assess pain and mobility every 6–12 months.
Encourage low‑impact aerobic activity (walking, swimming).
Educate on joint protection and proper footwear.
Monitor for progression to surgical thresholds.
Rheumatoid arthritis – inflammatory, symmetrical, morning stiffness >1 h.
Septic arthritis – acute, febrile, purulent effusion.
Gout – intermittent monoarthritis with urate crystals.
Meniscal tear – joint line tenderness, mechanical locking.
Early OA may have normal X‑ray; rely on clinical picture.
Joint fluid may be non‑inflammatory yet infection can still be present in immunocompromised patients.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe joint swelling with fever
Rapid loss of function or inability to bear weight
Unexplained night pain waking the patient

faq.q: Why does pain improve with rest?
faq.a: Mechanical loading stresses damaged cartilage; stopping activity reduces stress and pain.
Yes, usually secondary to trauma, metabolic disease, or infection.
Joint replacement relieves pain and restores function but does not reverse disease elsewhere.

exam: Describe the radiographic criteria used to stage knee osteoarthritis.
List three modifiable risk factors and explain how they influence disease progression.
